messages.content: Why does my function keep remembering values from previous calls? I wrote def add_item(item, items=[]): items.append(item); return items

That's the mutable default argument trap. Python evaluates default values once, when the function is defined, not each time it's called, so every call that doesn't pass its own list shares the same list object. The usual fix is to use None as the default and create the list inside: def add_item(item, items=None): if items is None: items = []; items.append(item); return items. Use the same pattern for dicts and sets. Immutable defaults such as numbers, strings and tuples are safe because they can't be changed in place.
What's the difference between git merge and git rebase?

Both bring work from one branch into another, but they record history differently. Merge keeps both lines of history and adds a merge commit that joins them, so nothing existing is rewritten. Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, which gives a straight line of history but creates new commit hashes. Because rebase rewrites commits, avoid it on branches other people have already pulled. A common habit is to rebase your own local feature branch to stay current, then merge it into main.
Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in Python?

Python stores floats in binary, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one. The stored values are slightly off, so the sum comes out as 0.30000000000000004. Compare floats with math.isclose(a, b) instead of ==, or use the decimal module when you need exact decimal arithmetic, such as for money.
whats the actual difference between a process and a thread? i keep mixing them up

A process is a running program with its own private memory space. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and all threads in one process share that process's memory. Sharing makes threads cheap to create and easy to communicate between, but it also means two threads can modify the same data at once and cause race conditions. Separate processes are better isolated, so one crashing usually doesn't take down the others, but they need explicit mechanisms like pipes or sockets to exchange data. One Python-specific note: in standard CPython the global interpreter lock stops threads from running Python bytecode in parallel, so CPU-heavy work usually needs multiple processes.
why is the sky blue

Sunlight contains all colors, and the atmosphere scatters short wavelengths like blue far more strongly than long ones like red, a process called Rayleigh scattering. That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky. Violet scatters even more, but the sun emits less of it and our eyes are less sensitive to it.
Why do I procrastinate on things I actually care about? I'll do the boring stuff instantly but put off my thesis for weeks.

There are a few plausible explanations, and they can overlap. When something matters, every attempt becomes a test of how good you are, so starting means risking a disappointing result, while boring tasks carry no verdict. Another possibility is that the thesis is simply vague: 'work on thesis' isn't something you can finish in an afternoon, whereas 'reply to email' is. It may also just be size, since big work needs a block of energy that never seems available. You can sort out which applies by noticing what happens when you sit down. If you feel dread about quality, lower the standard for the first session and write a deliberately bad page. If you feel lost, spend 20 minutes defining the next concrete step, like drafting the outline of one section. If you feel overwhelmed, commit to 25 minutes and allow yourself to stop afterward. The boring tasks aren't proof that you're lazy; they show you can act when the task is clear and the stakes are low, so the goal is to make the thesis look more like that.
I keep looking at my ex's Instagram even though I don't want to. What's wrong with me?

Nothing unusual is wrong with you. Checking is often an attempt to get information that would settle something, like whether they're doing fine without you or whether the breakup was as final as it felt, and a profile never answers that, so the urge renews itself. Each check also sometimes delivers something, a new photo or a new person, and unpredictable payoffs make habits stick. You'll likely get further by adding friction than by relying on willpower: mute or remove the account so looking takes effort, and move the app off your home screen for a few weeks. If you notice what you're hoping to find when you open it, that may tell you what you're actually missing.
Do I actually want to become a surgeon or do I just like the idea of people being impressed?

Probably some of both, which is common and not disqualifying; most career choices mix real interest with wanting respect. What matters is the proportion, and you can test it. Imagine nobody ever learned your job title: would you still want the long training, the night shifts and the daily work itself? Then look at the actual days rather than the title. Shadow a surgeon for a few days if you can, or read firsthand accounts of residency, and pay attention to whether the work interests you or only the status around it. If the routine tasks leave you flat while the title still appeals, that's useful information.
Why do I stay up late scrolling when I'm exhausted?

Often it's because that late hour is the first stretch of the day that belongs entirely to you, so you spend it even at the cost of sleep. Scrolling also asks nothing of you, which is appealing when you're tired. If that fits, giving yourself some unscheduled time earlier in the evening tends to work better than telling yourself to stop.
I always say yes to people and then resent them for it. Why do I do that?

Saying yes is the quicker way out of an awkward moment, and the cost arrives later, when you're tired and doing something you never wanted to do. The resentment is useful information, though: it usually means you had a limit that nobody knew about because you never stated it. The anger lands on them, but the decision was yours, which is uncomfortable to admit and also the helpful part, since it means you can change the pattern. Try buying time before answering with something like 'Let me check my schedule and get back to you.' That removes the pressure to decide on the spot, and you can then say yes to the things you mean and decline the rest without a long explanation. Expect some people to be briefly surprised; that usually passes.
Is it wrong to lie to protect someone's feelings?

Sometimes it's harmless and sometimes it does damage, so the answer depends on what the lie protects. Telling a nervous friend that their haircut looks fine is a different act from telling them their business plan is sound when you think it will fail. The first spares a small hurt, while the second takes away information they need for a decision and treats them as someone who can't handle reality. There's also a cost that accumulates: if you lie kindly, your praise becomes worth less, because they can't tell which compliments are real. Often the choice isn't between a lie and a wound; you can say something true and selective, like praising what actually works and being clear about the real problem. Some cases remain hard, such as a dying person asking a question with no good answer, and I'd be wary of anyone whose rule claims to settle all of them.
Do we have free will?

It depends heavily on what you mean by free will, and much of the long argument is really about that definition. If it means your choices are not caused by anything, including your brain, your history and your circumstances, the case for it looks weak. If it means you can deliberate, weigh reasons and act on them without coercion, then compatibilists, a large group of philosophers, say we have it even in a world where events have causes. Others reject that and think real responsibility requires more. Neither side has a knockdown argument, so it's better held as an open question than a settled one.
Everyone in my class cheats on the online quizzes. If I don't, I'm just handicapping myself. Isn't it fair to cheat too?

Your worry is legitimate, since grading on a curve can punish honest students, so I won't pretend the cost to you is imaginary. But the argument that everyone else does it proves less than it seems. It explains why you're tempted; it doesn't make the act fair, only spreads the unfairness around. Also check the premise: 'everyone' is rarely literally everyone, and you mostly notice the confident people. Practical options are to talk to the instructor about how the quizzes are set up, since many will change the format if they know it's being gamed, or to accept a possibly lower mark while you actually learn the material. Whether to join in is your decision, but I'd make it based on what you want to be responsible for, not on what the rest of the class is doing.
Can people really change or are we basically stuck with who we are?

Both are true to different degrees. Studies of personality traits find them fairly stable over decades, but they also drift: on average people become more conscientious and emotionally steady with age, and individuals vary a lot. Behavior changes more easily than temperament. A naturally anxious person usually doesn't become carefree, but they can learn to handle situations they once avoided. The most reliable changes tend to come from altering circumstances and habits, such as the people you spend time with and your daily routines, rather than from a decision to be different. So you're not stuck, but change is slower and more specific than the stories we tell about it.

i have eggs, rice and half an onion. dinner ideas?

Egg fried rice. Fry the chopped onion in a little oil until soft, push it aside, scramble two eggs in the same pan, then add the cold rice and stir everything together with salt and pepper, or a splash of soy sauce if you have it. Day-old rice works best because it's drier and won't turn mushy.
tell me a joke about programmers
A programmer's partner says, 'Go to the shop and buy a loaf of bread, and if they have eggs, get a dozen.' The programmer comes back with twelve loaves. 'They had eggs,' he explains.
Is a hot dog a sandwich?

By the dictionary definition, probably yes: filling inside bread. By the way people actually use the word, no, and language follows usage more than definitions. I'd call it a sandwich that has earned its own category.
My best friend hasn't replied to my texts in two weeks and I think she's mad at me. I keep going over what I might have done.

Two weeks of silence is unsettling, and it makes sense that your mind keeps searching for a cause. Still, silence has many explanations, such as a bad stretch at work, a family problem, or a person who goes quiet when overwhelmed, and anger is only one possibility. Since you can't tell which it is from the outside, replaying old conversations is unlikely to give you an answer. A short message tends to do more: something like 'Hey, I've missed you and wanted to check you're doing okay. No pressure to reply fast.' It doesn't accuse her of anything, and it leaves her room to answer however she can. If you do remember something specific that might have upset her, you can add one line about it, but I wouldn't invent an offense to apologize for.
failed my driving test for the third time today. feel so stupid

That's a frustrating way to end the day. Failing three times says something about the test conditions and your preparation, not about your intelligence; driving tests are partly about nerves, and many people need several attempts. If the examiner gave you a feedback sheet, look at what specifically cost you points, because that's usually a few fixable habits rather than a general inability. A session or two with an instructor focused on exactly those things, ideally on the local test routes, is often the cheapest way to fix them.
My roommate keeps eating my food and I don't want to make it a big deal. How do I bring it up?

Raising it early is how you keep it small; it becomes a big deal when you wait until you're furious. Keep it short and specific: 'Hey, I've noticed some of my food has been disappearing, like the yogurt and bread last week. Could you check with me before you take anything?' Starting with what you've seen, instead of calling it stealing, gives them a chance to say 'oh, sorry, I thought that was shared.' If you're fine with them using some things, say which ones, since a clear rule is easier to follow than a vague complaint. If it continues after that, a separate shelf or a small lockable box for your things is a reasonable next step.
My grandmother died last week and everyone keeps telling me she's in a better place. I just feel numb.

I'm sorry about your grandmother. Numbness after a death is a common reaction, and it doesn't mean you didn't love her or that something is wrong with you; sometimes the mind takes a loss in stages. You also don't owe anyone a particular feeling at a particular time, including the people offering comforting phrases that don't fit. It may help to have one person you can be honest with, who won't tell you how to feel. If the numbness lasts for many weeks and gets in the way of daily life, or feels worse instead of easing, talking to a doctor or counselor is a sensible step, but nothing you've described sounds out of the ordinary. Small things connected to her, like looking through photos or cooking something she made, can sometimes bring feelings up gently when you're ready.
How do I start waking up at 5am?

First check whether you need 5am or simply more time before the day gets busy, because for many people the benefit comes from the quiet hours, not the number on the clock. If you do want it, move your wake time earlier by 15 minutes every few days instead of jumping from 8 to 5, and shift your bedtime too, since you can't cut sleep without paying for it later. Put the alarm across the room, get light and water soon after waking, and have a specific thing to do, because getting up for nothing is hard to repeat. If you're naturally a late sleeper, forcing it may make you miserable, and a 6:30 start you can sustain beats a 5:00 start you abandon after a week.
I want to learn guitar but I only have 15 minutes a day. Is that pointless?

Not at all. Fifteen focused minutes daily beats a two-hour session once a week, because frequent short practice builds finger strength and memory faster. Spend it on one or two specific things, like a chord change or a short riff, instead of just playing what you already know.
Every Sunday I make a huge plan for the week and by Wednesday I've dropped it. what am I doing wrong

The plan is probably written for a version of you with a perfect week, and Wednesday is when the real one shows up with a late meeting and low energy. Plans that collapse usually have too many items, no slack, and no answer to what happens when you fall behind. Try cutting the list to three things that matter, leaving about a third of your available time unscheduled, and deciding in advance what the minimum version of each task is for a bad day, such as 10 minutes instead of an hour. Then on Wednesday you can do the small version and the plan survives. Also look at what you dropped first; if it's always the same kind of task, it may be something you don't actually want to do, and that deserves a separate decision.
I'm 24 and I feel like I haven't achieved anything. Everyone my age seems to be ahead.

What you're seeing is a comparison between your whole, unedited life and other people's highlights, which isn't a fair test. Timelines vary enormously: some people get early success and others settle into their work in their thirties, and 24 is early in either case. That said, the feeling may be pointing at something real, so it's worth separating two things: are you unhappy with the direction you're taking, or only with the pace compared with others? If it's direction, pick one thing you'd like to be noticeably better at a year from now and work out what the next few months of effort would look like. If it's only pace, then the comparison is what needs adjusting, which is easier to say than do, so consider spending less time on the accounts that make you feel behind.
I have two job offers. One pays 30% more at a boring company, the other pays less at a startup I'm excited about. How do I decide?

Start with the numbers, because 'pays less' needs to be compared with your actual needs: if the lower salary still covers your rent, debts and some savings, the gap is a preference; if it doesn't, it's a constraint, and that settles a lot. Then ask what each job will do for you in three years. A startup can offer broader responsibility and faster learning, but it can also fold, so ask about funding, how many months of runway they have, and whether the equity has any realistic value; treat equity as a lottery ticket, not income. For the boring company, find out whether boring means stable and well run or simply a place where you'll stagnate. Excitement is real information, but it's often highest before the first day, so talk to people who work at both places about what their days look like. If you're still split, which one would you regret not having tried?
I keep reorganizing and color-coding my notes instead of actually studying and my exam is in 5 days. Why and what do I do?

Reorganizing notes feels like studying because it involves the material and produces something visible, but it mostly trains recognition, which is much easier than recall, and recall is what the exam will ask for. It's also a low-effort activity that lets you feel productive while avoiding the harder work of testing yourself, which is a common trap, not a character flaw. With five days left, stop reorganizing today. Turn each section of your notes into questions, then close the notes and answer them from memory, marking what you missed. Redo the missed ones the next day. If past papers exist, do them under time limits, since that's the closest thing to the real exam. It will feel worse than rereading because you'll see your gaps, but that discomfort is the part that works.
A teammate in my group project keeps presenting my work as his. Should I confront him or just let it go since it's only one project?

Letting it go is reasonable if it's truly a one-off and the grade isn't affected, but check that assumption, because this kind of behavior tends to continue if nobody says anything, and it matters if the project is graded individually or if the instructor judges contribution. I'd talk to him privately first, without accusing him of bad motives: 'In the presentation, the analysis section was mine and it came across as yours. Can we make sure everyone's contributions get named next time?' He may be careless rather than malicious, and that approach gives him a chance to correct it. Meanwhile, keep records, such as drafts and messages that show who did what, so you can demonstrate your contribution if it becomes a dispute. If he brushes it off, raise it with the instructor using those records, and describe what happened rather than what you suspect he intended.
I want to quit social media but my friends plan everything there and I'm scared I'll get left out.

That concern deserves to be taken seriously, because the social cost is real and the fear isn't irrational. But the choice isn't all or nothing. You could delete the apps from your phone while keeping the accounts, checking them once a day from a computer, which removes most of the compulsive use while keeping you reachable. Or tell your closest friends you're stepping back and ask them to text you about plans; people who care usually adapt, and how they react will tell you which friendships depended on the platform. Try it for a month with a clear question, such as whether you feel better and whether you actually missed anything, then decide from what happened instead of from the prediction. The fear of missing out is often bigger in anticipation than in practice, though you may find that one particular group really does coordinate only there, and then you'll have to decide how much that matters.
